patient.name: Terence Whitlock
patient.complaint: A painful sore on the outer ankle that will not heal, worse at night

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a leg or foot ulcer: the site, the edge, the pain and the pulses decide arterial versus venous, neuropathic or pressure ulcer.

points: Terence, 71, has a sore on his **right outer ankle** for 6 weeks.
It is **very painful**, worst at night in bed.
He sleeps in the chair with his leg hanging down.
For two years his **calf aches after 100 m**, eased by rest.

steps.lead: Terence's sore sits on a limb with poor blood flow: an ulcer from **tissue ischaemia** due to peripheral arterial disease.
Terence collects nearly every PAD driver: **smoking**, diabetes, hypertension and untreated high cholesterol.

visual.title: How far Terence can walk before calf pain
visual.caption: A shrinking claudication distance, then **rest pain** and an ulcer: arterial disease getting worse.

points: Right foot is **cold and pale**; no foot pulses felt.
Shin skin is **thin and shiny**, with no hair.
Foot turns pale when raised and **red when hanging down**.
Ulcer over the **lateral malleolus**: small, deep, sharp-edged.

steps.lead: Terence has the full picture: lateral malleolus site, **pain at rest**, claudication, cold pulseless foot and chronic ischaemic skin changes.
His ulcer is **'punched out'** with a dry, pale base that barely bleeds: the signature arterial look.

steps.q: Terence's ulcer is deep, punched out, on the lateral malleolus, with absent pulses. Which ulcer is it?
steps.r: Punched-out edge, painful, distal site, cold pulseless foot: **arterial**. Venous ulcers are shallow, sloping and over the medial malleolus.

steps.title: Arterial vs venous vs neuropathic ulcer
head: Feature
Arterial
Venous
Neuropathic

steps.text: Pain eased by **hanging the leg down** is arterial (gravity helps flow). Pain eased by **elevation** is venous. The stem often hides this in how the patient sleeps.

steps.lead: Without blood supply Terence's ulcer can progress to **gangrene**, critical limb ischaemia and **amputation**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (pulses and ABPI) or the investigation before intervention (CT angiography), plus questions on what an ABPI value means.

steps.q: Terence's foot pulses are absent. What is the first-line bedside test?
steps.r: Palpate pulses, then measure the **ABPI**. CT angiography comes later to plan revascularisation.

steps.lead: In clinic the nurse feels for Terence's pulses and measures his **ABPI** with a Doppler and cuff.

steps.title: Terence's ABPI
steps.text: ABPI = ankle systolic ÷ highest brachial systolic. 72 ÷ 160 = 0.45.

visual.title: ABPI
visual.label: Terence 0.45
visual.caption: Below **0.8** is significant arterial disease; below **0.5** suggests critical limb ischaemia.

steps.lead: Terence's right ABPI of **0.45** is below 0.5: with rest pain and an ulcer, this is critical limb ischaemia.

steps.text: In diabetes, calcified arteries can make the ABPI **falsely normal or high** (above 1.3). A 'normal' ABPI with absent pulses still needs imaging.

steps.lead: To plan treatment, Terence has **CT angiography**, the gold standard: it shows where his arteries are blocked.

steps.text: **ABPI** tells you how bad; **CT angiography** tells you where. Never put a compression bandage on a leg before checking the ABPI.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (smoking cessation, exercise, clopidogrel, atorvastatin) and 'next step' questions where critical ischaemia needs revascularisation.

steps.q: Which treatment would harm Terence's ulcer?
steps.r: **Compression** is for venous ulcers and is dangerous with an ABPI below 0.8: it further cuts arterial flow.

steps.lead: Terence starts on the basics: **stop smoking**, supervised exercise, **clopidogrel** and **atorvastatin**.
His night pain needs **analgesia**: paracetamol first, escalating to an opioid such as morphine for severe rest pain.

points: CT angiography: **occluded right superficial femoral artery**.
Rest pain and an ulcer: critical limb ischaemia.

steps.lead: Tissue loss and an ABPI of 0.45 mean Terence needs **revascularisation**: angioplasty or bypass surgery.

steps.title: Arterial ulcer pathway
steps.caption: No compression at any point while the ABPI is low.

visual.title: After Terence's angioplasty
visual.caption: Restore the blood supply and the ulcer can finally heal.

steps.text: Arterial ulcers heal only when **perfusion** improves. Dressings alone will not heal an ulcer on a leg with no blood supply.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why arterial ulcers appear at the toes and lateral malleolus, why the foot reddens when dependent, and why antiplatelets and statins are given.

steps.lead: Atheroma in Terence's femoral artery critically reduces perfusion, so the most **distal** tissue at his ankle breaks down first.

steps.title: From atheroma to ulcer
nodes: Distal and watershed skin becomes ischaemic

steps.lead: Terence's ulcer has sharp, **punched-out** edges because a discrete patch of tissue died from focal ischaemia.
His thin, shiny, hairless shin is **atrophy** from chronic ischaemia; the red dependent foot is **dependent rubor**.

steps.q: Why does Terence's foot turn red when he hangs it down?
steps.r: **Dependent rubor**: arterioles are maximally dilated to compensate for ischaemia, so gravity fills them red. Haemosiderin is venous.

steps.lead: Terence's ABPI measured how bad his disease is; his CT angiogram showed **where** it was so the team could plan angioplasty.
Clopidogrel and atorvastatin lower Terence's risk of **progression**, MI and stroke: his legs reflect his coronary and carotid arteries.

mcq.q: Where do arterial ulcers classically occur?
mcq.r: Distal, poorly perfused sites: **toes, heel, lateral malleolus**. Medial malleolus is venous.

mcq.q: What is the classic appearance of an arterial ulcer?
mcq.r: Well-defined **punched-out** edges, deep, dry pale base with minimal bleeding.

mcq.q: Which describes the pain of an arterial ulcer?
mcq.r: Arterial ulcers are **painful even at rest**, often eased by hanging the leg down.

mcq.q: Which is a chronic skin change of arterial insufficiency?
mcq.r: **Hair loss, shiny thin skin** and dependent rubor. The others are venous.

mcq.q: Which ABPI value is diagnostic of significant arterial disease in the notes?
mcq.r: ABPI **<0.8** = significant arterial disease; <0.5 suggests critical limb ischaemia.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard investigation for an arterial ulcer?
mcq.r: **CT angiography** maps the arterial blockage before intervention.

mcq.q: Which antiplatelet is named first-line in PAD?
What is the definitive treatment for an arterial ulcer?

mcq.r: Ischaemic vessels dilate maximally to compensate; when dependent, gravity fills them red.

prompts.q: What is an arterial ulcer and what are its risk factors?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem lists the vascular risk factors to point you to arterial.

points.p: Ulcer from tissue ischaemia due to reduced arterial supply (PAD)
points.why: The cause is poor inflow, not venous back-pressure.
The strongest modifiable PAD risk factor.
Diabetes also causes neuropathic ulcers, so check sensation.
The usual atherosclerosis drivers.

prompts.q: Describe the classic site, appearance and symptoms of an arterial ulcer.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: site, edge, base, pain.

points.why: Medial malleolus points to venous.
Sloping irregular edges are venous.

points.p: Dry base, pale surrounding skin, minimal bleeding
points.why: Venous ulcers are wet and exudative.
Rest pain signals critical ischaemia.
Walking pain relieved by rest is the PAD history.

prompts.q: What do you find on examining the limb with an arterial ulcer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: list the signs of chronic ischaemia.

points.p: Cold limb with reduced or absent pulses
points.why: Strong pulses make arterial unlikely.
Atrophic change from chronic ischaemia.
Pale on elevation, red when dependent.
Below 0.5 suggests critical limb ischaemia.

prompts.q: Which features tell you an ulcer is arterial rather than venous?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the classic SBA puts both in the options.

points.p: Site: lateral malleolus/toes vs medial malleolus/gaiter
points.why: Venous: gaiter area above the medial malleolus.

points.p: Edge: punched out vs irregular sloping
points.why: Venous are shallow and irregular.

points.p: Pulses absent, ABPI low vs pulses present
points.why: Venous ulcers have palpable pulses.

points.p: Pale shiny skin vs haemosiderin and lipodermatosclerosis
points.why: Brown staining and induration are venous.

prompts.q: What complications follow an untreated arterial ulcer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: it is a limb-threatening progression.

points.why: Dry gangrene of the toes is the classic next stage.
Rest pain or tissue loss with ABPI usually <0.5.
Non-viable tissue cannot be saved.

prompts.q: What is the first-line investigation and what do the ABPI cut-offs mean?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bedside first, then the number.

points.why: Done before anything else.
Ankle systolic divided by brachial systolic.
Also the threshold below which compression is unsafe.
Needs urgent vascular referral.

prompts.q: What is the gold-standard investigation and why is it done?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the test before intervention.

points.why: Not venous duplex, which is for venous disease.

points.p: Shows location and extent of arterial blockage to plan revascularisation
points.why: ABPI gives severity; CTA gives anatomy.

prompts.q: What is the first-line, second-line and definitive management of an arterial ulcer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: risk factors and drugs, then pain, then restore flow.

points.p: Smoking cessation and supervised exercise programme
points.why: Lifestyle comes first in every PAD question.
Reduces cardiovascular events.
Lipid-lowering for every patient with PAD.
Rest pain can be severe.
The only way the ulcer will heal in critical ischaemia.

prompts.q: Which venous-ulcer treatment must you avoid in an arterial ulcer, and why?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a classic harmful distractor.

points.why: It is the venous ulcer treatment.

points.p: Unsafe when ABPI is low (<0.8): further reduces arterial flow
points.why: Always check ABPI before compression.

prompts.q: Why do arterial ulcers occur where they do, look punched out and cause dependent rubor?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: explain each sign from ischaemia.

points.p: Critically reduced perfusion from atherosclerotic PAD
points.why: Inflow failure.
Toes, heel and lateral malleolus.

points.p: Punched out: discrete area of tissue death from focal ischaemia
points.why: Hence sharp edges.

points.p: Dependent rubor: maximally dilated vessels compensating
points.why: Gravity fills them when the leg hangs down.

points.p: Antiplatelet and statin reduce atherosclerotic progression and CV events
points.why: PAD predicts coronary and cerebral disease.

glossary.arterial ulcer: A skin ulcer caused by poor arterial blood supply, usually from peripheral arterial disease.
glossary.PAD: Peripheral arterial disease: atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries to the limbs.
glossary.peripheral arterial disease: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the legs, reducing blood flow.
glossary.ischaemia: Inadequate blood supply to a tissue, starving it of oxygen.
glossary.atherosclerosis: Build-up of fatty plaque in artery walls, narrowing them.
glossary.atheroma: The fatty plaque inside an artery wall in atherosclerosis.
glossary.punched out: Describes an ulcer with sharp, well-defined, vertical edges, like a hole punch.
glossary.lateral malleolus: The bony bump on the outer side of the ankle (end of the fibula).
glossary.medial malleolus: The bony bump on the inner side of the ankle (end of the tibia).
glossary.gaiter area: The lower leg between the ankle and mid-calf, where venous ulcers form.
glossary.claudication: Cramping leg pain on walking caused by ischaemia, relieved by rest.
glossary.intermittent claudication: Calf pain brought on by walking a predictable distance and relieved by rest.
glossary.rest pain: Ischaemic pain at rest, often at night, a sign of critical limb ischaemia.
glossary.dependent rubor: Redness of the foot when it hangs down, from maximally dilated ischaemic vessels.
glossary.ABPI: Ankle-brachial pressure index: ankle systolic pressure divided by brachial systolic pressure.
glossary.ankle-brachial pressure index: Ratio of ankle to arm systolic blood pressure; low values mean arterial disease.
glossary.critical limb ischaemia: Severe PAD with rest pain, ulcers or gangrene, often ABPI below 0.5.
glossary.CT angiography: CT scan with IV contrast that shows the arteries and where they are blocked.
glossary.Doppler: Handheld ultrasound probe used to hear arterial flow and measure ankle pressure.
glossary.revascularisation: Restoring blood flow to a limb by angioplasty or bypass surgery.
glossary.angioplasty: Widening a narrowed artery from inside with a balloon, sometimes with a stent.
glossary.bypass: Surgery that routes blood around a blocked artery using a vein or graft.
glossary.gangrene: Death of body tissue from loss of blood supply, sometimes with infection.
glossary.amputation: Surgical removal of a limb or part of a limb.
glossary.clopidogrel: Antiplatelet drug that blocks the P2Y12 receptor, used in PAD.
glossary.atorvastatin: Statin that lowers cholesterol and stabilises atherosclerotic plaques.
glossary.antiplatelet: Drug that stops platelets clumping, reducing arterial clots.
glossary.statin: Cholesterol-lowering drug that inhibits HMG-CoA reductase.
glossary.venous ulcer: Shallow, irregular ulcer over the medial malleolus caused by chronic venous hypertension.
glossary.neuropathic ulcer: Painless ulcer on pressure points of the sole due to loss of sensation, often diabetic.
glossary.haemosiderin: Iron pigment from broken-down red cells that stains the skin brown in venous disease.
glossary.lipodermatosclerosis: Hard, tight, inflamed skin of the lower leg from chronic venous disease.
glossary.compression bandaging: Firm layered bandaging for venous ulcers; unsafe if arterial supply is poor.
glossary.superficial femoral artery: The main thigh artery, a common site of PAD occlusion.
glossary.watershed: Tissue at the far end of an arterial territory, most vulnerable to low flow.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man has a 4 week history of a painful ulcer on the tip of his left big toe. The pain is worse at night and eased by hanging his leg out of bed. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day. The ulcer is deep with a well-defined, punched-out edge and a pale, dry base. The foot is cool and pedal pulses are not palpable.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a leg ulcer: decide by site, edge, pain and pulses.

clues: tip of his left big toe
worse at night and eased by hanging his leg out of bed
steps.x: Distal site, **rest pain** eased by dependency, smoker, punched-out edge and absent pulses: all arterial.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Painful punched-out toe ulcer in a pulseless foot: **arterial ulcer**.

elim: Neuropathic ulcers are **painless** and on the sole's pressure points.
Pressure ulcers sit over bony prominences in immobile patients.
Pyoderma has an undermined violaceous edge and normal pulses.
Venous ulcers are shallow, sloping, medial malleolus, with pulses present.

steps.x: **A. Arterial ulcer.** Rule: punched out + painful at rest + no pulses = arterial.

technique.stem: A 68 year old woman has a painful ulcer on her right heel. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and a 30 pack-year smoking history. She describes calf pain after walking 50 m. The right foot is pale and cool with no palpable pulses. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: It asks for the **initial** investigation, not the gold standard.

clues: painful ulcer on her right heel
steps.x: Heel ulcer, claudication and absent pulses: suspected arterial ulcer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line is pulses then **ABPI** at the bedside.

elim: She has no fever or sepsis; cultures do not assess perfusion.
CT angiography is the gold standard **before intervention**, not first.
MRI looks for osteomyelitis, not arterial supply.
Venous duplex is for venous disease.

steps.x: **A. Ankle-brachial pressure index.** Initial = ABPI; planning = CT angiography.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has a painful punched-out ulcer over his left lateral malleolus. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and takes no regular medication. Pedal pulses are absent and his left ABPI is 0.7. CT angiography shows diffuse disease not suitable for intervention at present.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management of an arterial ulcer.

clues: punched-out ulcer over his left lateral malleolus
steps.x: Arterial ulcer, active smoker, no statin, ABPI below 0.8, no revascularisation yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line: **risk factor control**, antiplatelet and statin.

elim: Compression is for venous ulcers and dangerous when ABPI <0.8.
No signs of infection are described.
Amputation is for non-viable tissue, not a first step.
Steroids treat pyoderma or eczema, not ischaemia.

steps.x: **D.** First-line = stop smoking, exercise, clopidogrel and atorvastatin.

technique.stem: A 72 year old man with peripheral arterial disease has a non-healing ulcer on his right fourth toe. When he lies down his foot becomes white; when he sits with it hanging over the bed it turns deep red. His foot pulses are absent.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the red colour when his foot hangs down?
o: Maximal compensatory dilatation of ischaemic vessels

steps.x: A mechanism question about a sign: **dependent rubor**.
Pallor on elevation, redness when dependent, in PAD: dependent rubor.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ischaemic arterioles are **maximally dilated** to compensate; gravity fills them.

elim: Haemosiderin gives fixed brown staining in venous disease.
Infection would not change colour with posture.
Polycythaemia gives generalised plethora, not postural.
Thrombophlebitis is a tender red cord along a vein.

steps.x: **C.** Dependent rubor = maximally dilated, poorly functioning vessels.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man has a 5 week history of a painful ulcer on the tip of his right second toe. He has angina and smokes 25 cigarettes a day. The right foot is paler and cooler than the left. The ulcer is small, deep and well defined with a pale base and no bleeding. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 152/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A painful, deep, well-defined toe ulcer with a pale base in a cool foot is arterial. Venous ulcers are shallow, medial and exudative.

steps.x: Ulcer diagnosis: use site, edge, base and pain.

clues: painful ulcer on the tip of his right second toe
deep and well defined with a pale base
steps.x: Distal toe, painful, smoker with vascular disease, cold pale foot, punched-out look.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Arterial ulcer.**

elim: Neuropathic ulcers are painless and on the sole.
No immobility or bony prominence.
Pyoderma has a violaceous undermined edge.
Venous ulcers are shallow, sloping and over the medial malleolus.

steps.x: **A.** Painful, punched out, distal, pale = arterial.

practice.stem: A 73 year old woman has a punched-out ulcer over her left lateral malleolus. She has type 2 diabetes and hypercholesterolaemia and smoked for 40 years. She has calf pain after walking 100 m. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 148/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her left leg?
o: Haemosiderin staining of the gaiter area
Pale foot on elevation that reddens when dependent
Varicose veins along the medial thigh
practice.e: Arterial insufficiency gives pallor on elevation and dependent rubor. The other options are signs of chronic venous disease.

steps.x: A finding question: first name the condition, then its sign.

clues: punched-out ulcer over her left lateral malleolus
steps.x: Punched-out lateral ulcer plus claudication: arterial ulcer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Arterial signs: cold, pulseless, hairless shiny skin, **dependent rubor**.

elim: Atrophie blanche is a venous skin change.
Haemosiderin staining is venous.
Lipodermatosclerosis is venous.
Varicose veins point to venous disease.

steps.x: **D.** Dependent rubor is the arterial sign; the rest are venous.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has worsening right calf pain on walking for 3 years and now has pain in his right foot at night. He smokes and has hypertension. The right foot is cold with absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. The skin of the shin is shiny and hairless.
practice.q: Which is the most likely site for an ulcer to develop?
o: Gaiter area above the medial malleolus
Plantar surface of the first metatarsal head
practice.e: Arterial ulcers form at distal, poorly perfused sites: toes, heel and lateral malleolus. The gaiter area is venous; the metatarsal head is neuropathic.

steps.x: Where will an ulcer form? Identify the disease first.

clues: pain in his right foot at night
absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
steps.x: Claudication progressing to rest pain with ischaemic skin: PAD.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Arterial ulcer sites: **toes, heel, lateral malleolus**.

elim: Gaiter area is the venous site.
Medial calf is not a typical arterial ulcer site.
Plantar metatarsal head is the neuropathic pressure point.
Sacrum is a pressure ulcer site.

steps.x: **B. Lateral malleolus.** Medial = venous, lateral = arterial.

practice.stem: A 77 year old man has a painful, deep ulcer on his left heel and pain in the foot every night for 4 weeks. He has a 50 pack-year smoking history. The left foot is cold and pale with no palpable pulses. There is no gangrene. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 160/92 mmHg.
practice.q: Which best describes the severity of his arterial disease?
practice.e: Rest pain and an ulcer with ABPI below 0.5 is critical limb ischaemia. Acute ischaemia is sudden, over hours, with the 6 Ps.

steps.x: A severity question: use the symptoms and the ABPI.

clues: painful, deep ulcer on his left heel
pain in the foot every night for 4 weeks
steps.x: Tissue loss and **rest pain** over weeks; ABPI 0.40.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ABPI <0.5 with rest pain or ulcer: **critical limb ischaemia**.

elim: Acute ischaemia is sudden (hours), not 4 weeks.
He has rest pain and tissue loss, beyond claudication.
0.40 is far below mild.
ABPI below 0.8 is significant disease.

steps.x: **B. Critical limb ischaemia.** ABPI <0.5 + rest pain or ulcer.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has a painful ulcer on his right fifth toe. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Sensation to monofilament is normal. The ulcer has a punched-out edge with a dry base. The foot is cool with absent pulses.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his ulcer?
o: Narrowing of leg arteries by atheroma
practice.e: Normal sensation, absent pulses and a painful punched-out ulcer mean ischaemia from atherosclerotic PAD, not neuropathy.

steps.x: Cause of the ulcer: arterial, venous, neuropathic or pressure?

clues: painful ulcer on his right fifth toe
punched-out edge with a dry base
steps.x: Diabetic, but sensation is intact and the ulcer is painful: not neuropathic. Pulseless foot: arterial.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Atherosclerotic PAD** causing tissue ischaemia.

elim: Venous hypertension gives shallow medial ulcers with pulses present.
Monofilament sensation is normal and the ulcer hurts.
Toe tip is not a pressure site in a mobile man.
No rash, systemic features or normal pulses to suggest vasculitis.

steps.x: **C.** Arterial ulcer = ischaemia from atheroma narrowing the arteries.

practice.stem: A 79 year old man has had a painful arterial ulcer on his left big toe for 3 months. He continued to smoke and declined vascular review. Over 2 weeks the toe has become black, dry, shrivelled and painless with a clear line between it and the healthy pink skin. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg.
practice.e: An arterial ulcer can progress to gangrene. Dry, black, painless tissue with a clear demarcation and no fever is dry gangrene.

steps.x: A complication of an arterial ulcer.

clues: clear line between it and the healthy pink skin
steps.x: Mummified, demarcated, afebrile.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ischaemic progression: **dry gangrene**.

elim: Cellulitis is red, hot and spreading.
Gas gangrene follows trauma with crepitus and sepsis.
Osteomyelitis is bone infection; the toe would not mummify.
Wet gangrene is moist, painful, foul, febrile and poorly demarcated.

steps.x: **B. Dry gangrene.** Arterial ulcer → gangrene → amputation.

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman has a painful, deep ulcer over her right lateral malleolus with pain at night. She smokes and has hypertension. The right foot is cool. The GP cannot feel her foot pulses. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 144/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: First-line is pulses and ABPI at the bedside. CT angiography is the gold standard before intervention, not the first test.

steps.x: **Initial** investigation, so a bedside test.

clues: painful, deep ulcer over her right lateral malleolus
steps.x: Suspected arterial ulcer; pulses already checked.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Next is the **ABPI**.

elim: Gold standard, used to plan revascularisation after ABPI.
An X-ray does not assess blood supply.
Venous duplex is for venous ulcers.
No signs of infection; a swab does not explain the ulcer.

steps.x: **A. ABPI.** Pulses, then ABPI, then CT angiography.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man has a non-healing arterial ulcer on his left heel. His left ABPI is 0.42 and he has rest pain. The vascular surgeon is planning revascularisation and wants to know the site and extent of the arterial blockage.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: CT angiography is the gold standard to map arterial disease before angioplasty or bypass. Repeating the ABPI gives severity, not anatomy.

steps.x: Which test maps the arteries before intervention?

clues: site and extent of the arterial blockage
steps.x: Severity is already known; the surgeon needs anatomy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT angiography**, the gold standard. Normal eGFR makes contrast safe.

elim: Already done; it gives severity, not location.
No sepsis is described.
Assesses neuropathy, not arteries.
Assesses veins, not arterial occlusion.

steps.x: **C.** ABPI = how bad; CT angiography = where.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has a painful punched-out ulcer on his right heel. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and takes ramipril only. The right foot is cool with absent pulses. His right ABPI is 0.65. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Elevation of the leg above the heart
practice.e: First-line for an arterial ulcer is risk factor control with an antiplatelet and statin. Compression and elevation suit venous ulcers and worsen ischaemia.

steps.x: Initial management of an arterial ulcer.

clues: punched-out ulcer on his right heel
steps.x: Arterial ulcer, smoker, raised LDL, not on antiplatelet or statin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop smoking, exercise, **clopidogrel**, **atorvastatin**.

elim: Compression is unsafe with ABPI below 0.8.
Elevation worsens arterial flow and pain.
No infection is described.
Steroids do not treat ischaemia.

steps.x: **D.** Risk factors plus antiplatelet and statin.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman has an arterial ulcer on her left big toe and severe pain at night. She stopped smoking and takes clopidogrel and atorvastatin. Regular paracetamol has not controlled the pain and she cannot sleep. She has no history of peptic ulcer. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 142/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step for her pain?
practice.e: Arterial ulcer pain escalates from paracetamol to opioid analgesia such as morphine for severe pain. Ischaemic rest pain is not neuropathic.

steps.x: Pain control after paracetamol has failed.

clues: Regular paracetamol has not controlled the pain
steps.x: Severe ischaemic rest pain despite step 1.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Escalate to an **opioid**, e.g. morphine (and push for revascularisation).

elim: Amitriptyline is for neuropathic pain.
NSAIDs are not the notes' escalation and carry renal and GI risk.
Steroids have no role in ischaemic pain.
Topical lidocaine will not touch deep ischaemic rest pain.

steps.x: **C. Morphine.** Paracetamol, then opioid for severe pain.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has a non-healing arterial ulcer on his right lateral malleolus and rest pain despite stopping smoking, clopidogrel and atorvastatin. The foot is viable. CT angiography shows a short occlusion of the right superficial femoral artery.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has an arterial ulcer on the tip of his left big toe. He smokes and has peripheral arterial disease. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg. The student asks why the ulcer has formed at the toe tip rather than higher up the leg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Chronic venous back-pressure is highest in the toes
Distal tissue is the last to be perfused and ischaemic first
Loss of sensation lets the toes be injured
practice.e: Reduced arterial perfusion hits the most distal, watershed tissue first: toes, heel and lateral malleolus break down.

steps.x: A mechanism question about the site of an arterial ulcer.

clues: tip of his left big toe
steps.x: PAD and the most distal point of the limb.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Distal/watershed** tissue becomes ischaemic first.

elim: Venous back-pressure causes gaiter-area ulcers.
That is the neuropathic mechanism.
Pressure alone does not explain an ischaemic ulcer.
Not a recognised mechanism.

steps.x: **B.** The furthest tissue from the heart suffers first.
